messages.body_plain:
Thanks Daniel, this helps me understand the implications of the changes. There are a few aspects of partial ID SCR models that I've found no other way to implement in nimble than to "hack" the system a bit to make them work. Regarding this "hack" specifically, I want nimble to automatically set up samplers as if the capture history is data and then I replace the update for the latent capture histories. This is more or less how it worked before with the exception that nimble specified a posterior predictive update for the latent capture histories that I then replaced. Also, I could see all the samplers.

After the change, it appears that I can just set the upstream posterior predictive branch samplers for parameters back to what they would have been assigned if the capture histories were not latent (or whatever else might be more appropriate) in addition to replacing the update for the latent capture histories and it will work as it did before.That appears to be the case comparing some posteriors across versions of nimble for the same data sets.

You are correct that you need to see the custom capture history update to see how these apparently disjoint graphs are connected. The first model I mentioned is more or less this model (https://www.pnas.org/content/117/30/17903.short) for genotypes with Normal partial ID covariates instead of categorical ones. The only other difference is that this specific model is built on the Royle-Young (2008) SCR model instead of the most common SCR model. I've previously implemented the genotype version in nimble using the same "hacks" and the results match those from my R-based sampler so I'm quite confident nimble was doing what I intended. It looks like I should test this again with the newest version of nimble.

Thanks again,

Ben

On Tue, Oct 26, 2021 at 9:31 PM Daniel Turek <db...@williams.edu> wrote:
> Ben, let me explain briefly about the (newly introduced) posterior predictive branch sampler (hereafter: "branch sampler"), and what I'm seeing from your model.
>
> The branch sampler was introduced in nimble version 0.11.1, to jointly sample trailing branches of the model which contain no data whatsoever.  These branches are thus jointly-posterior-predictive.  That is, say there's a model with node x, and y depends on x, and z depends on y, but *none* of x, y, or z are data (information flows as x -> y -> z, or if arrows denote dependence upon, then x <- y <- z).  Then, instead of (previous nimble behaviour) assigning RW or perhaps conjugate samplers to x and y, and a posterior predictive sampler to z, it would make sense to jointly sample (x,y,z) by calling the simulate methods (in order) of each of these nodes.  Since none of them are data, we can simulate x (conditional on everything "upwards" in the model that x depends on), then simulate y (conditional on the new value of x), and finally simulate z (conditional on the new value of y).  That's essentially how the branch sampler operates.  (Noting, and we've seen one case of this before, where user-defined distributions which may/may not have a simulation function ("r"-distribution), the branch sampler might not play nicely in this instance, and that's something that might need attention).
>
> Also worth noting, for the model structure above, the old nimble behaviour would assign (and print) samplers along the lines of:
> RW samplers: x and y
> posterior predictive sampler: z
> Clearly showing how nimble plans on updating each of x, y, and z.
>
> The new nimble behaviour, using the new branch sampler, which perhaps could be improved, now only shows:
> branch sampler: x
> And it's left somewhat unclear to understand that internal to this branch sampler on x is sampling the whole branch following from entirely-non-data branch point (x), and everything downstream of it (y, z) internal to the sampler.  So, point being, in printing the samplers you wouldn't actually see anything "assigned' to sample y or z.
>
> Looking into your model, at least from your first two emails, was a little difficult since I couldn't create the model (missing the constants and data, in particular), and also I"m missing the custom functions and distributions you're using (of which there are several).
>
> That said, I tried to study the dependence structure carefully, and also gleaned a few clues from your print-outs of the sampler assignments (from versions 0.10 and 0.11).  Critically, understanding the dependency structure is important for thinking about the branch sampler.
>
> As best I can tell from looking at this output, it seems like the model has two *disjoint* graphs:
> psi, p, sigma, s, z, u, available, y.true
> If (as I suspect) *none* of these quantities are specified as data (excluding "available" which is deterministic), then here's what you're seeing for this first disjoint graph:
> Nothing is data.
> Every "top" node is a branch point for exclusively non-data dependencies (those being: psi, p, sigma, s)
> Therefore, a branch sampler is assigned to each of: psi, p, sigma, s - exactly what you're seeing, under version 0.11, per your 4th email.
>
> There's another (entirely disjoint) graph in your model:
> G.mu, G.tau, G.true, tau.obs, G.obs
> The dependence structure culminates in G.obs; and no samplers are ever assigned to G.obs, so I infer G.obs is assigned as data.  Since these nodes (G.mu, G.tau, G.true, tau.obs) all have trailing data beneath them in the dependency structure (that being: G.obs), there are no branch nor posterior predictive samplers assigned in this 2nd disjoint graph, and other samplers are assigned (e.g., RW, conjugate), and operate as you'd expect on G.mu, G.tau, tau.obs, etc.
>
> I will not claim to fully understand your model, but I'm suspicious about these two *entirely disjoint* graphs making up your model.  Is it possible there's intended to be some sort of dependence upon the 1st graph (including, perhaps, y.true) existing in the 2nd graph (perhaps in the, data G.obs)?  If so, then the data G.obs would actually influence estimation of top parameters such as psi, p, sigma, etc.  This dependence in G.obs could be manifested as dependence on any of the quantities derived from y.true, as well, for example capcounts, or quite simply "n", being used anywhere in the 2nd graph.
>
> Anyway, as it stands: you're seeing branch samplers assigned to psi, p, sigma, and s, because they have no data depending on them in the graphical structure.  Internal to each of these branch samplers, for example that assigned to sigma, nimble calls the simulate methods of (sigma, u, available (which is a deterministic calculation of the value), and y.true).  And this also explains your observation about no sampler being assigned to "z", because the branch sampler assigned to psi, internally, calls the simulation methods of (psi, z, y.true).
>
> I also recognize the possibility that this missing "dependency" between the graphs actually exists in the custom sampler you've written, and that you're assigning to y.true.  That's an advanced use of the system, and could be perfectly valid, but the default sampler assignments certainly would not detect that.  Please let me know if that's the case, which would be something else to think about.
>
> I also admit, I did not study the other model ("similar sampler for SCR with unknown left and right flank linkages") from your 3rd email.  I'm hoping I've explained enough about the branch sampler, that your questions about that model will now make sense.
>
> Anyway, this was long-winded, but I tried to explain about the new branch sampler, and explain some of your (and my) observations about your model and the sampler assignments.  Please take your time reading through this and parsing it, and hopefully it makes sense.
>
> If you still have other questions, don't hesitate to follow up further.
>
> Cheers,
> Daniel
>
>

messages.body_plain:
A brief additional note: You can turn off the newer posterior branch sampling scheme that Daniel described by doing:
setNimbleOption('MCMCjointlySamplePredictiveBranches', FALSE)
I believe this is intended to  give you the old behavior, which might let you move ahead with the system you've set up.

On Tue, Oct 26, 2021 at 7:56 PM Ben Augustine <baug...@vt.edu> wrote:

> Thanks Daniel, this helps me understand the implications of the changes. There are a few aspects of partial ID SCR models that I've found no other way to implement in nimble than to "hack" the system a bit to make them work. Regarding this "hack" specifically, I want nimble to automatically set up samplers as if the capture history is data and then I replace the update for the latent capture histories. This is more or less how it worked before with the exception that nimble specified a posterior predictive update for the latent capture histories that I then replaced. Also, I could see all the samplers.
>
> After the change, it appears that I can just set the upstream posterior predictive branch samplers for parameters back to what they would have been assigned if the capture histories were not latent (or whatever else might be more appropriate) in addition to replacing the update for the latent capture histories and it will work as it did before.That appears to be the case comparing some posteriors across versions of nimble for the same data sets.
>
> You are correct that you need to see the custom capture history update to see how these apparently disjoint graphs are connected. The first model I mentioned is more or less this model (https://www.pnas.org/content/117/30/17903.short) for genotypes with Normal partial ID covariates instead of categorical ones. The only other difference is that this specific model is built on the Royle-Young (2008) SCR model instead of the most common SCR model. I've previously implemented the genotype version in nimble using the same "hacks" and the results match those from my R-based sampler so I'm quite confident nimble was doing what I intended. It looks like I should test this again with the newest version of nimble.
>
> Thanks again,
>
> Ben
>
>
>
> On Tue, Oct 26, 2021 at 9:31 PM Daniel Turek <db...@williams.edu> wrote:
> > Ben, let me explain briefly about the (newly introduced) posterior predictive branch sampler (hereafter: "branch sampler"), and what I'm seeing from your model.
> >
> > The branch sampler was introduced in nimble version 0.11.1, to jointly sample trailing branches of the model which contain no data whatsoever.  These branches are thus jointly-posterior-predictive.  That is, say there's a model with node x, and y depends on x, and z depends on y, but *none* of x, y, or z are data (information flows as x -> y -> z, or if arrows denote dependence upon, then x <- y <- z).  Then, instead of (previous nimble behaviour) assigning RW or perhaps conjugate samplers to x and y, and a posterior predictive sampler to z, it would make sense to jointly sample (x,y,z) by calling the simulate methods (in order) of each of these nodes.  Since none of them are data, we can simulate x (conditional on everything "upwards" in the model that x depends on), then simulate y (conditional on the new value of x), and finally simulate z (conditional on the new value of y).  That's essentially how the branch sampler operates.  (Noting, and we've seen one case of this before, where user-defined distributions which may/may not have a simulation function ("r"-distribution), the branch sampler might not play nicely in this instance, and that's something that might need attention).
> >
> > Also worth noting, for the model structure above, the old nimble behaviour would assign (and print) samplers along the lines of:
> > RW samplers: x and y
> > posterior predictive sampler: z
> > Clearly showing how nimble plans on updating each of x, y, and z.
> >
> > The new nimble behaviour, using the new branch sampler, which perhaps could be improved, now only shows:
> > branch sampler: x
> > And it's left somewhat unclear to understand that internal to this branch sampler on x is sampling the whole branch following from entirely-non-data branch point (x), and everything downstream of it (y, z) internal to the sampler.  So, point being, in printing the samplers you wouldn't actually see anything "assigned' to sample y or z.
> >
> > Looking into your model, at least from your first two emails, was a little difficult since I couldn't create the model (missing the constants and data, in particular), and also I"m missing the custom functions and distributions you're using (of which there are several).
> >
> > That said, I tried to study the dependence structure carefully, and also gleaned a few clues from your print-outs of the sampler assignments (from versions 0.10 and 0.11).  Critically, understanding the dependency structure is important for thinking about the branch sampler.
> >
> > As best I can tell from looking at this output, it seems like the model has two *disjoint* graphs:
> > psi, p, sigma, s, z, u, available, y.true
> > If (as I suspect) *none* of these quantities are specified as data (excluding "available" which is deterministic), then here's what you're seeing for this first disjoint graph:
> > Nothing is data.
> > Every "top" node is a branch point for exclusively non-data dependencies (those being: psi, p, sigma, s)
> > Therefore, a branch sampler is assigned to each of: psi, p, sigma, s - exactly what you're seeing, under version 0.11, per your 4th email.
> >
> > There's another (entirely disjoint) graph in your model:
> > G.mu, G.tau, G.true, tau.obs, G.obs
> > The dependence structure culminates in G.obs; and no samplers are ever assigned to G.obs, so I infer G.obs is assigned as data.  Since these nodes (G.mu, G.tau, G.true, tau.obs) all have trailing data beneath them in the dependency structure (that being: G.obs), there are no branch nor posterior predictive samplers assigned in this 2nd disjoint graph, and other samplers are assigned (e.g., RW, conjugate), and operate as you'd expect on G.mu, G.tau, tau.obs, etc.
> >
> > I will not claim to fully understand your model, but I'm suspicious about these two *entirely disjoint* graphs making up your model.  Is it possible there's intended to be some sort of dependence upon the 1st graph (including, perhaps, y.true) existing in the 2nd graph (perhaps in the, data G.obs)?  If so, then the data G.obs would actually influence estimation of top parameters such as psi, p, sigma, etc.  This dependence in G.obs could be manifested as dependence on any of the quantities derived from y.true, as well, for example capcounts, or quite simply "n", being used anywhere in the 2nd graph.
> >
> > Anyway, as it stands: you're seeing branch samplers assigned to psi, p, sigma, and s, because they have no data depending on them in the graphical structure.  Internal to each of these branch samplers, for example that assigned to sigma, nimble calls the simulate methods of (sigma, u, available (which is a deterministic calculation of the value), and y.true).  And this also explains your observation about no sampler being assigned to "z", because the branch sampler assigned to psi, internally, calls the simulation methods of (psi, z, y.true).
> >
> > I also recognize the possibility that this missing "dependency" between the graphs actually exists in the custom sampler you've written, and that you're assigning to y.true.  That's an advanced use of the system, and could be perfectly valid, but the default sampler assignments certainly would not detect that.  Please let me know if that's the case, which would be something else to think about.
> >
> > I also admit, I did not study the other model ("similar sampler for SCR with unknown left and right flank linkages") from your 3rd email.  I'm hoping I've explained enough about the branch sampler, that your questions about that model will now make sense.
> >
> > Anyway, this was long-winded, but I tried to explain about the new branch sampler, and explain some of your (and my) observations about your model and the sampler assignments.  Please take your time reading through this and parsing it, and hopefully it makes sense.
> >
> > If you still have other questions, don't hesitate to follow up further.
> >
> > Cheers,
> > Daniel

Regarding this "hack" specifically, I want nimble to automatically set up samplers as if the capture history is data and then I replace the update for the latent capture histories. This is more or less how it worked before with the exception that nimble specified a posterior predictive update for the latent capture histories that I then replaced. Also, I could see all the samplers.
> >
> > After the change, it appears that I can just set the upstream posterior predictive branch samplers for parameters back to what they would have been assigned if the capture histories were not latent (or whatever else might be more appropriate) in addition to replacing the update for the latent capture histories and it will work as it did before.That appears to be the case comparing some posteriors across versions of nimble for the same data sets.
> >
> > You are correct that you need to see the custom capture history update to see how these apparently disjoint graphs are connected. The first model I mentioned is more or less this model (https://www.pnas.org/content/117/30/17903.short) for genotypes with Normal partial ID covariates instead of categorical ones. The only other difference is that this specific model is built on the Royle-Young (2008) SCR model instead of the most common SCR model. I've previously implemented the genotype version in nimble using the same "hacks" and the results match those from my R-based sampler so I'm quite confident nimble was doing what I intended. > > > Ben, let me explain briefly about the (newly introduced) posterior predictive branch sampler (hereafter: "branch sampler"), and what I'm seeing from your model.
> > >
> > > The branch sampler was introduced in nimble version 0.11.1, to jointly sample trailing branches of the model which contain no data whatsoever.  These branches are thus jointly-posterior-predictive.  That is, say there's a model with node x, and y depends on x, and z depends on y, but *none* of x, y, or z are data (information flows as x -> y -> z, or if arrows denote dependence upon, then x <- y <- z).  Then, instead of (previous nimble behaviour) assigning RW or perhaps conjugate samplers to x and y, and a posterior predictive sampler to z, it would make sense to jointly sample (x,y,z) by calling the simulate methods (in order) of each of these nodes.  Since none of them are data, we can simulate x (conditional on everything "upwards" in the model that x depends on), then simulate y (conditional on the new value of x), and finally simulate z (conditional on the new value of y).  That's essentially how the branch sampler operates.  (Noting, and we've seen one case of this before, where user-defined distributions which may/may not have a simulation function ("r"-distribution), the branch sampler might not play nicely in this instance, and that's something that might need attention).
> > >
> > > Also worth noting, for the model structure above, the old nimble behaviour would assign (and print) samplers along the lines of:
> > > RW samplers: x and y
> > > posterior predictive sampler: z
> > > Clearly showing how nimble plans on updating each of x, y, and z.
> > >
> > > The new nimble behaviour, using the new branch sampler, which perhaps could be improved, now only shows:
> > > branch sampler: x
> > > And it's left somewhat unclear to understand that internal to this branch sampler on x is sampling the whole branch following from entirely-non-data branch point (x), and everything downstream of it (y, z) internal to the sampler.  So, point being, in printing the samplers you wouldn't actually see anything "assigned' to sample y or z.
> > >
> > > Looking into your model, at least from your first two emails, was a little difficult since I couldn't create the model (missing the constants and data, in particular), and also I"m missing the custom functions and distributions you're using (of which there are several).
> > >
> > > That said, I tried to study the dependence structure carefully, and also gleaned a few clues from your print-outs of the sampler assignments (from versions 0.10 and 0.11).  Critically, understanding the dependency structure is important for thinking about the branch sampler.
> > >
> > > As best I can tell from looking at this output, it seems like the model has two *disjoint* graphs:
> > > psi, p, sigma, s, z, u, available, y.true
> > > If (as I suspect) *none* of these quantities are specified as data (excluding "available" which is deterministic), then here's what you're seeing for this first disjoint graph:
> > > Nothing is data.
> > > Every "top" node is a branch point for exclusively non-data dependencies (those being: psi, p, sigma, s)
> > > Therefore, a branch sampler is assigned to each of: psi, p, sigma, s - exactly what you're seeing, under version 0.11, per your 4th email.
> > >
> > > There's another (entirely disjoint) graph in your model:
> > > G.mu, G.tau, G.true, tau.obs, G.obs
> > > The dependence structure culminates in G.obs; and no samplers are ever assigned to G.obs, so I infer G.obs is assigned as data.  Since these nodes (G.mu, G.tau, G.true, tau.obs) all have trailing data beneath them in the dependency structure (that being: G.obs), there are no branch nor posterior predictive samplers assigned in this 2nd disjoint graph, and other samplers are assigned (e.g., RW, conjugate), and operate as you'd expect on G.mu, G.tau, tau.obs, etc.
> > >
> > > I will not claim to fully understand your model, but I'm suspicious about these two *entirely disjoint* graphs making up your model.  Is it possible there's intended to be some sort of dependence upon the 1st graph (including, perhaps, y.true) existing in the 2nd graph (perhaps in the, data G.obs)?  If so, then the data G.obs would actually influence estimation of top parameters such as psi, p, sigma, etc.  This dependence in G.obs could be manifested as dependence on any of the quantities derived from y.true, as well, for example capcounts, or quite simply "n", being used anywhere in the 2nd graph.
> > >
> > > Anyway, as it stands: you're seeing branch samplers assigned to psi, p, sigma, and s, because they have no data depending on them in the graphical structure.  Internal to each of these branch samplers, for example that assigned to sigma, nimble calls the simulate methods of (sigma, u, available (which is a deterministic calculation of the value), and y.true).  And this also explains your observation about no sampler being assigned to "z", because the branch sampler assigned to psi, internally, calls the simulation methods of (psi, z, y.true).
> > >
> > > I also recognize the possibility that this missing "dependency" between the graphs actually exists in the custom sampler you've written, and that you're assigning to y.true.  That's an advanced use of the system, and could be perfectly valid, but the default sampler assignments certainly would not detect that.  Please let me know if that's the case, which would be something else to think about.
> > >
> > > I also admit, I did not study the other model ("similar sampler for SCR with unknown left and right flank linkages") from your 3rd email.  I'm hoping I've explained enough about the branch sampler, that your questions about that model will now make sense.
> > >
> > > Anyway, this was long-winded, but I tried to explain about the new branch sampler, and explain some of your (and my) observations about your model and the sampler assignments.  Please take your time reading through this and parsing it, and hopefully it makes sense.
> > >

> > >
> > > Cheers,

messages.body_plain:
Dear Vicky,

Sounds interesting.  Each of constant, cancerdata, and Istinits should be a named list.  It sounds like you have cancerdata as an array.  The names of the list elements for any of those three arguments should correspond to variable names in your model code.

>From your description, I think you would want data = list(O = cancerdata[1:67, 1]), so that you build the model with one data set to start.

After you build and compile the model and MCMC algorithm, you can assign new values to any data variables.  For example, if you have done

compiled_ICARmodel <- compileNimble(ICARmodel)

then you can do

compiled_ICARmodel$O <- cancerdata[1:67, 2]

to set the values of O in the model to your second data set (if I follow).  To do this, the sizes (N and L in your model) must not change.  If they change, you would need to re-do nimbleModel and compileNimble.

For further steps and nimble basics, I'll refer you to our user manual at r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org>.  It looks like you're just getting started and so that might be useful for you.  Let us know further questions.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Solved!

Needed to index y with [[]] instead of [,1].

covVals2 <- nimbleFunction(
run = function(y = double(2),
S = double(2),
cov1= double(1),
cov2 = double(1),
cov3 = double(1)) {

dist <- matrix(0, nrow = length(S[,1]), ncol=length(y[[1]]))

for(i in 1:length(S[,1])) {

dist[i,] <- sqrt(((y[[1]] - S[i, 1]) ^2) + ((y[[2]] - S[i, 2]) ^2)) #calculate nearest

}
id <- which(dist == min(dist))

x1.val <- cov1[id]
x2.val <- cov2[id]
x3.val <- cov3[id]

cov.vals <- array(c(x1.val, x2.val, x3.val), dim = c(3, length(y[[1]])))
return(cov.vals)
returnType(double(2))
}
)

bla <- data.frame(array(0, c(3, 5)))
for (t in 2:length(test2mu[,1])) {
bla[t] <- covVals2(test2mu[t-1,1:2], testS, xTest1, xTest2, xTest3)
}

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rowenna,

You shouldn't need (or want) to use double brackets in a nimbleFunction.  Does that compile?

I think the possible confusion is that when you provide y[t-1, 1:2] as an argument for covVals2 in your model code, that creates a vector (not a matrix) because the first index is a single value.  So the argument type to covVals2 should be "y = double(1)", not "y = double(2)".  Does that work?

Also it is important to test this using compiled code to ensure the types work as intended.  I couldn't quite tell if you are testing these uncompiled or compiled.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Enrico,

I haven't gone through this completely thoroughly, but here is what I am seeing. I hope that this information will allow you to work out a solution, and I'm happy to discuss this further here.

If you use x ~ T(dsome_density(a,b),m,M), nimble calculates the density as the original density dsome_density(a,b) divided by the probability of a value less than M minus the probability of a value less than m. I.e., we normalize the original density by the probability of being in the interval (m,M).  This is done on the log scale as the log of the original density minus the log of the difference in probabilities, where those probabilities are calculated on the original (non-log) scale.

In some cases in your problem, as the MCMC is starting to take samples (probably in the first or second iteration) it looks like a value mu[i] is a negative number that is fairly large in magnitude (e.g., -400). In that case, because the density is concentrated at large magnitude negative values, the two probabilities we are subtracting are both numerically equal to 1 and so the difference is 0.  The result is that you have some density divided by 0, which is Infinity, for theta[i]. This then causes all sorts of weird things to happen with whether proposals are accepted.

I don't know that it will fix things in this case, but in general, for numerical accuracy, it's best to calculate the various quantities in your d,p,q functions on the log scale and then only if log=FALSE exponentiate the result, rather than calculating on the original scale and then taking the log if log=TRUE. In this case, given how far 1 and 55000 can be into the right tail, this might still end up giving you probabilities that are exactly 1.

One other thought is that it seems like a value of mu[i] that is, say, -400 is not a reasonable parameter value (particularly given the sigma and tau values) given that the thetas are positive. So perhaps different initial values for alpha and beta would make sense, or constraints or different priors for alpha and beta.

On the nimble side, we may want to think harder about making sure that when this happens with T() that it is handled more robustly, perhaps such that the density evaluates to 0 instead of Inf and therefore that proposals that lead to this would be rejected.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Apologies - I spoke too soon - I thought it was on it's way to compiling but there is an error.

Here is my modified code:

covVals2 <- nimbleFunction(
run = function(y = double(1),

S = double(2),
cov1= double(1),
cov2 = double(1),
cov3 = double(1)){
dist <- matrix(0, nrow = length(S[,1]), ncol=length(y[,1]))
for(i in 1:length(S[,1])) {
dist[i,] <- sqrt(((y[,1] - S[i, 1]) ^2) + ((y[,2] - S[i, 2]) ^2)) #calculate nearest
}

id <- which(dist == min(dist))

x1.val <- cov1[id]
x2.val <- cov2[id]
x3.val <- cov3[id]

cov.vals <- array(c(x1.val, x2.val, x3.val), dim = c(3, length(y[,1])))
return(cov.vals)
returnType(double(2))
}
)

Hi Chris,

Many thanks for this - it all makes sense. And indeed it happens only with either bad priors or very long chains (I initially discovered this with longer chains of 2 million iterations). I was also playing around and noticed this happens with other distributions as well (see examples below, my concerns are the two examples in the middle). I ended using a work-around by expanding artificially the interpolation range and then adding a dconstraint which fixed my specific problem, but will definitely update my d,p,q functions. Thanks!

All Best,

Enrico

###

library(nimble)
library(truncnorm)
obs.theta <- 14
sim  <-  nimbleCode({theta ~ T(dnorm(mean=0,sd=1),m,M)})
nimbleModel(sim,constant=list(m=-Inf,M=Inf),data=list(theta=obs.theta))$logProb_theta #returns # -98.91894
log(dtruncnorm(obs.theta,mean=0,sd=1)) #returns  -98.91894

#m=10
nimbleModel(sim,constant=list(m=10,M=Inf),data=list(theta=obs.theta))$logProb_theta #returns +Inf
log(dtruncnorm(obs.theta,mean=0,sd=1,a=10)) #returns -Inf

#m=10, M=15
nimbleModel(sim,constant=list(m=10,M=15),data=list(theta=obs.theta))$logProb_theta #returns +Inf
log(dtruncnorm(obs.theta,mean=0,sd=1,a=10,b=15)) #returns -1.609438

#m=15, M=30
nimbleModel(sim,constant=list(m=15,M=30),data=list(theta=obs.theta))$logProb_theta #returns -Inf
log(dtruncnorm(obs.theta,mean=0,sd=1,a=15,b=30)) #returns -Inf

On 28/10/2021 02:09, Chris Paciorek wrote:
> Hi Enrico,
>
> I haven't gone through this completely thoroughly, but here is what I am seeing. I hope that this information will allow you to work out a solution, and I'm happy to discuss this further here.
>
> If you use x ~ T(dsome_density(a,b),m,M), nimble calculates the density as the original density dsome_density(a,b) divided by the probability of a value less than M minus the probability of a value less than m. I.e., we normalize the original density by the probability of being in the interval (m,M).  This is done on the log scale as the log of the original density minus the log of the difference in probabilities, where those probabilities are calculated on the original (non-log) scale.
>
> In some cases in your problem, as the MCMC is starting to take samples (probably in the first or second iteration) it looks like a value mu[i] is a negative number that is fairly large in magnitude (e.g., -400). In that case, because the density is concentrated at large magnitude negative values, the two probabilities we are subtracting are both numerically equal to 1 and so the difference is 0.  The result is that you have some density divided by 0, which is Infinity, for theta[i]. This then causes all sorts of weird things to happen with whether proposals are accepted.
>
> I don't know that it will fix things in this case, but in general, for numerical accuracy, it's best to calculate the various quantities in your d,p,q functions on the log scale and then only if log=FALSE exponentiate the result, rather than calculating on the original scale and then taking the log if log=TRUE. In this case, given how far 1 and 55000 can be into the right tail, this might still end up giving you probabilities that are exactly 1.
>
> One other thought is that it seems like a value of mu[i] that is, say, -400 is not a reasonable parameter value (particularly given the sigma and tau values) given that the thetas are positive. So perhaps different initial values for alpha and beta would make sense, or constraints or different priors for alpha and beta.
>
> On the nimble side, we may want to think harder about making sure that when this happens with T() that it is handled more robustly, perhaps such that the density evaluates to 0 instead of Inf and therefore that proposals that lead to this would be rejected.

> -chris

messages.subject: Re: nimble function - issues with indexing
messages.body_plain:
It looks like something is still not right about dimensions (number of indices) of y.

I don't know if I misread your code in my previous reply.  Somewhere I thought I saw you trying to provide y as an argument to covVals2 as a vector.  But the way it is used inside of covVals2, it does look like you want it to be a matrix.  I may have been hasty.

I am a little lost at this point on exactly what you need, but maybe we can still see a solution.  Daniel's code provided above can be compiled with the following modification:

id[i] <- which(dist[,i] == min(dist[,i]))[1]

The reason this didn't compile as it was written is that `which` returns a vector, but id[i] is a scalar.  nimbleFunctions become statically typed when they compile, so types need to match, and this can be confusing in some cases.  Adding [1] at the end ensures that the type of the result will be a scalar.

(Also there is a missing comma in
x1 = runif(200, 0, 1000)
)

So now you are back to y being a matrix, which I think is what you wanted.

Thanks Daniel for putting together that code.

Also it is better to do dim(X)[1] instead of length(x[,1]) because the latter will make a copy of x[,1] just for the purpose of determining its length.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Perry - thanks for circling back to this again!

What I really want to do is use the covVals function in a nimble model with a loop over the locations. The reason I want to do this is because I'm estimating the locations (they are the latent state) and would like to use the previous location (y_t-1) to get the covariate value and use that in an equation to estimate the next location.

e.g.

for (t in 2:length(y[,1])) {

covar[t] <- covVals2(y[t-1,1:2], testS, xTest1, xTest2, xTest3)
}

Daniel's code (thank you again) works but I believe only if you are supplying all of the y values at once as a matrix and doesn't work in a loop like above.

You did see in my initial code that did try to define y as double(2) but even when I edit it to double(1) I'm still getting the indexing error when I compile. Am I right in thinking that stochastic indexing isn't supported by nimble?

Thank you again for your help on this!
Rowenna

On Thu, 28 Oct 2021 at 16:46, Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> It looks like something is still not right about dimensions (number of indices) of y.
>
> I don't know if I misread your code in my previous reply.  Somewhere I thought I saw you trying to provide y as an argument to covVals2 as a vector.  But the way it is used inside of covVals2, it does look like you want it to be a matrix.  I may have been hasty.
>
> I am a little lost at this point on exactly what you need, but maybe we can still see a solution.  Daniel's code provided above can be compiled with the following modification:
>
> id[i] <- which(dist[,i] == min(dist[,i]))[1]
>
> The reason this didn't compile as it was written is that `which` returns a vector, but id[i] is a scalar.  nimbleFunctions become statically typed when they compile, so types need to match, and this can be confusing in some cases.  Adding [1] at the end ensures that the type of the result will be a scalar.
>
> (Also there is a missing comma in
> x1 = runif(200, 0, 1000)
> )
>
> So now you are back to y being a matrix, which I think is what you wanted.
>
> Thanks Daniel for putting together that code.
>
> Also it is better to do dim(X)[1] instead of length(x[,1]) because the latter will make a copy of x[,1] just for the purpose of determining its length.
>
> -Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rowenna,

I wrote some more simulation code and slicked out the function just a bit after you described exactly what you wanted to do.

Perry, thanks for the help and catching my coding errors. I need to slow down a bit here :)

I've included an example that compiles and runs the MCMC:

Hopefully this solves your problem:

x1 = runif(200, 0, 1000)

y1 = runif(200, 0, 1000)
pts = SpatialPoints(cbind(x1, y1))

rast = raster(xmn = 0, xmx = 1000, ymn = 0, ymx = 1000, res = 100)
rast[] = rpois(ncell(rast), 20)
rast1 = rast
rast1[] = rpois(ncell(rast), 20)
rast2 = rast
rast2[] = rpois(ncell(rast), 20)

#covariate function
covVals2 <- nimbleFunction(

  run = function(y = double(1),
                 S = double(2),
                 cov1= double(1),
                 cov2 = double(1),
                 cov3 = double(1)) {

    dist <- sqrt(((y[1] - S[1:dim(S)[1], 1]) ^2) + ((y[2] - S[1:dim(S)[1], 2]) ^2)) #calculate nearest

    # now loop over locations to get covariate ids

    id = which(dist == min(dist))

    x1.val <- cov1[id]
    x2.val <- cov2[id]
    x3.val <- cov3[id]

    cov.vals <- c(x1.val, x2.val, x3.val)
    return(cov.vals)
    returnType(double(1))
  }
)
# test the function with first point
covVals2(y = coordinates(pts)[1,], S = coordinates(rast), cov1 = rast@data@values, cov2 = rast1@data@values,cov3 = rast2@data@values)

# to simulate the problem in compilied code
nimcode <- nimbleCode({

  for(i in 1:nLocs){
  y[i,1] ~ dunif(0, 1000)
  y[i,2] ~ dunif(0, 1000)
  }
  for(i in 2:nLocs){
  covs[1:3,i] <- covVals2(y=y[i-1,],S=rast.coords[1:nRast,1:2], cov1 = v1[1:nRast], cov2 = v2[1:nRast], cov3 = v3[1:nRast])
  }
})

nimData = list(rast.coords = coordinates(rast),v1 = rast@data@values, v2 = rast1@data@values,v3 = rast2@data@values, covs = matrix(0, nrow=3, ncol=200))
constants = list(nLocs = 200, nRast = prod(dim(rast)[1:2]))

testR <- nimbleModel(nimcode,data = nimData, constants = constants, inits = list(y = matrix(runif(constants$nLocs*2),ncol=2)))

# complete initialization of model
testR$calculate()
testR$initializeInfo()

# compile model
testC <- compileNimble(testR, showCompilerOutput = FALSE)
# MCMC sampler configurations
mcmcspec<-configureMCMC(testR, monitors=c("y","covs"))
# build the MCMC specifications
testMCMC <- buildMCMC(mcmcspec)
# complile the code
CtestMCMC <- compileNimble(testMCMC, project = testR,resetFunctions = TRUE)
# run MCMC
tic()
samples <- runMCMC(CtestMCMC, niter = 10000, nburnin=1000,thin=1,nchains=1)
toc()

colNames <- grep("covs\\[",colnames(samples))
(covs <- samples[1,colNames]) # look at the first iteration

Rowenna

>

> > > > Rowenna

> > > > > id[i] <- which(dist[,i] == min(dist[,i]))[1]

Adding [1] at the end ensures that the type of the result will be a scalar.

> > > > > )

> > > > >

> > > > >
> > > > > -Perry
